what.text: Testosterone undecanoate is an ester of testosterone: testosterone with a long fatty-acid chain attached. The body cuts off that chain, which releases testosterone. It is the active ingredient of 3 oral capsules approved in the US (Jatenzo, Tlando, Kyzatrex) and of 1 injection given into the buttock muscle (Aveed).
How it acts, according to the FDA labels:

items.text: Once released, testosterone acts like the body’s own: it drives the growth of the male sex organs and keeps up male traits such as body hair, a deeper voice, and muscle and fat distribution.
Testosterone from outside the body signals the brain to cut its output of LH and FSH. With large doses this can suppress sperm production.

what.text: All 4 US brands are approved only for men whose low testosterone has a medical cause (hypogonadism). Their safety and efficacy in men with low testosterone due to age alone have not been established.

research.text: Each US brand was approved on an open-label trial in men with hypogonadism. The main measure was hormone levels: the share of men whose average testosterone landed in the normal range. These trials were not built to test symptoms, heart outcomes or fertility.

research.title: Oral Jatenzo vs a testosterone solution (Swerdloff et al.)

facts.v: 222 men aged 18 to 65 with hypogonadism: 166 on oral testosterone undecanoate (Jatenzo), 56 on a testosterone solution applied to the skin (Axiron)
average testosterone over 24 hours (Cavg); safety, including 24-h blood pressure

research.found: 87% of men in both groups had an average testosterone in the normal range. Safety looked similar between groups, but the oral product raised average systolic blood pressure by about 3 to 5 mm Hg. The study was funded by the maker (Clarus Therapeutics).

facts.v: Tlando 225 mg twice a day with food, no dose adjustment

research.found: 80% of men had an average testosterone in the normal range (300 to 1,080 ng/dL). A separate 4-month study in 138 men measured blood pressure.

facts.v: 155 men with hypogonadism; 139 in the efficacy analysis, median age 50
about 6 months, doses adjusted at days 28 and 56

research.found: 88% had an average testosterone in the normal range (222 to 800 ng/dL) at day 90. A 12-month open-label study in 212 men added safety data.

research.title: Aveed 84-week study

facts.v: 130 men with hypogonadism, mean age 54; 117 analysed after the third injection
Aveed 750 mg at the start, at 4 weeks, then every 10 weeks
average testosterone over the 10-week dosing interval

research.found: 94% had an average testosterone in the normal range (300 to 1,000 ng/dL); 5.1% were below and 0.9% above it. 7.7% had a peak above 1,500 ng/dL.

research.text: The labels report that testosterone from outside the body suppressed sperm production in rats, dogs and monkeys, and that this reversed when treatment stopped.

us.text: Testosterone undecanoate is FDA approved, as 4 brands, for men with hypogonadism. It is a Schedule III controlled substance. Aveed can be given only in certified healthcare settings under a REMS safety program. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: intramuscular injection, NDA 022219, approved March 5, 2014. Now held by Endo. Approved for adult men with primary or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and only when the benefit outweighs the serious risks of POME and anaphylaxis.
FDA’s data also lists a generic testosterone undecanoate injection (ANDA 207583, Hikma) with tentative approval only (December 2016), not as a marketed product.

src.label: Drugs@FDA data (openFDA), all testosterone undecanoate applications

items.text: all 4 labels say safety and efficacy have not been established in men with “age-related” (late-onset) hypogonadism or in males under 18. Use outside the labeled conditions is off-label.

Aveed is available only through the Aveed REMS Program. Prescribers and healthcare settings must be certified, and the setting must be able to manage POME and anaphylaxis. Patients are observed for 30 minutes after each injection.

on February 28, 2025, FDA told makers of all testosterone products to add TRAVERSE results, remove the boxed warning language about heart outcomes, and add or update warnings that testosterone can raise blood pressure. The current oral labels list blood pressure increases as a warning.

world.lead: Testosterone undecanoate is an approved prescription medicine in the US, Canada, the EU and Northern Ireland. In Europe the products listed are injections such as Nebido. Canada added Jatenzo, Kyzatrex and Tlando in 2026. It is banned in sport at all times.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Aveed injection, 2014; Jatenzo, Tlando and Kyzatrex capsules, 2019 to 2022) for male hypogonadism. Prescription-only; Schedule III.
Authorised medicine. Jatenzo (marketed April 2026) and Kyzatrex (marketed September 2026) capsules; Tlando approved September 29, 2026. Jatenzo is listed as a controlled drug (CDSA Schedule IV).

after.text: Australia’s Poisons Standard (October 2026) lists testosterone in Schedule 4 (prescription only) and in Appendix D, clause 5, for anabolic and androgenic steroids, which must not be possessed without authority under local law. The TGA’s register could not be reached to confirm which products are registered.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Testosterone is named under class S1.1, anabolic androgenic steroids, on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, when given from outside the body; the class covers its esters. S1 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) and its substances are non-Specified. Testosterone stays named in S1.1 on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027.

side.text: Aveed has a boxed warning for serious pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) reactions and anaphylaxis, which can be life-threatening. All 4 brands share testosterone’s class warnings: higher red cell counts, blood clots, blood pressure increases, prostate effects, and lower sperm production that may not reverse.

items.text: serious POME reactions (urge to cough, shortness of breath, throat tightening, chest pain, dizziness, fainting) and anaphylaxis have been reported during or just after the injection, after any dose including the first. In a review of 18 clinical trials with 3,556 men, 9 POME events in 8 men and 2 anaphylaxis events were judged to have occurred.

Jatenzo raised 24-h systolic/diastolic blood pressure by an average 4.9/2.5 mm Hg after 4 months, and blood pressure had not levelled off by the end of the trial. Aveed raised it by 3.1/2.0 mm Hg after 16 weeks. In TRAVERSE, a trial of testosterone gel in men with heart disease or risk factors, major heart events were 7% vs 7.3% on placebo.
testosterone can raise hematocrit (red cell mass), which may raise the risk of blood clots. Blood clots in the veins (DVT and pulmonary embolism) have been reported with testosterone products.
reduced fertility is seen in some men on testosterone. With large doses, sperm production may be suppressed, and the labels say the effect on fertility may be irreversible.

testosterone can worsen an enlarged prostate and may raise the risk of prostate cancer. It must not be used by men with breast cancer or known or suspected prostate cancer. In the Aveed trial, PSA rose above 4 ng/mL in 14 men (10.9%) who started below it.

acne, injection site pain and PSA increase were most common with Aveed. Headache, raised hematocrit and high blood pressure were most common with Jatenzo; high blood pressure and raised hematocrit with Tlando.
Jatenzo’s label warns that depression and suicidal thoughts were reported in its trials. Tlando’s label warns about raised prolactin.

swelling (edema), breast growth, sleep apnea, cholesterol changes, raised calcium and liver effects are listed warnings. Testosterone has been abused at high doses, with serious heart and mental health effects. It must not be used in pregnancy, because it can masculinize a female fetus.
